progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C12 (titration, burette, titre, endpoint and equivalence point; phenolphthalein's colourless to faint pink endpoint; the titre counts moles; n = cV). C10 (Ka, pKa = −log Ka; Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair). C08 (weak base: B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻, [OH⁻] = √(Kb × c) when Kb is small, then pOH and pH = 14.00 − pOH). C07 (pH, pOH, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, neutral pH 7.00 at 25 °C; the decimal-places rule). C06 (conjugate pairs; the conjugate base of a weak acid takes protons back, the conjugate base of a strong acid barely does; ammonium is ammonia's conjugate acid). C05 (strong and weak acids and bases; salts dissolve completely into ions). C11 (a weak acid with its conjugate base is a buffer; [H₃O⁺] = Ka × n(HA) ÷ n(A⁻); pH = pKa when the partners are equal). Module 5: Le Chatelier's principle. Not assumed: indicator, HIn, transition range, salt hydrolysis, the pH jump.
progression.startsWith: Observe a reversible indicator colour change. The video opens: Here's twenty five point zero zero millilitres of zero point one zero zero moles per litre ethanoic acid, titrated with sodium hydroxide of the same concentration. The moles say it needs twenty five millilitres. With phenolphthalein, that's what you get: the flask turns pink within a drop of twenty five.
progression.stopsAfter: describing an indicator as a weak acid whose two forms differ in colour; explaining its colour change, and its reversal, with Le Chatelier's principle; explaining why the change spans roughly two pH units around the indicator's pKa; stating four transition ranges; separating the endpoint from the equivalence point; predicting whether the solution at equivalence is acidic, neutral or basic from its salt, with an equation; calculating the equivalence pH of a weak acid with a strong base; choosing an indicator whose colour change falls inside the steep jump and explaining why a wrong choice gives a titre that is too small. No red cabbage preparation (chem-m6-p01), no whole-curve reading or conductivity (chem-m6-c14), no weak/weak titrations, no back titrations (chem-m6-c15).
progression.nextLesson: making an indicator from red cabbage and testing it with acids and bases (route chem-m6-p01).

teaching.task: The same titration needs twenty five millilitres of base, but methyl orange changes colour before eight. How does an indicator change colour, why isn't every equivalence point at pH 7, and how do you choose the indicator that changes at the right moment?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the same titration needs 25.00 mL by moles; phenolphthalein agrees, methyl orange drifts from red to yellow over the first 8 mL: why? (1); (2) an indicator is a weak acid whose acid and base forms differ in colour; the colour shows which form dominates (2); (3) base removes hydronium, so the equilibrium shifts right; acid shifts it back; the indicator is not used up, so the change is reversible (3); (4) the ratio of the two forms follows [H₃O⁺]; equal at the indicator's pKa; one colour is seen when one form is about ten times the other, so the change spreads over roughly two pH units (4); (5) the endpoint should land at equivalence, so you need the equivalence pH, and it is not always 7 (5); (6) at equivalence the flask holds sodium ethanoate; ethanoate, a weak acid's conjugate base, takes protons from water, making hydroxide: basic (6); (7) NaCl: neither ion reacts with water, neutral; NH₄Cl: ammonium gives protons to water, acidic (7); (8) the ethanoate concentration at equivalence: the volume doubled (8); (9) Kb = Kw ÷ Ka, the weak-base method, pOH, pH 8.72 (9); (10) near equivalence the pH leaps several units in a drop; phenolphthalein changes inside the leap; methyl orange changes in the buffer region, so its titre is far too small (10); (11) the rule: the change must fall inside the jump; for strong with strong the jump is long, so all three work (11); memory aid (12); two attempts and brief feedback (13 to 16); decision rule and handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: one puzzle carries the video: the same ethanoic acid titration needs 25.00 mL of base by moles, and phenolphthalein turns pink within a drop of that, but methyl orange drifts from red to yellow over the first 8 mL. The particle lens shows why: an indicator is itself a weak acid whose two forms have different colours, added base and acid shift its equilibrium back and forth, and the ratio of the two forms spreads the visible change over roughly two pH units around its pKa. The flask at equivalence holds a salt that takes after its stronger parent, a worked example finds pH 8.72 through Kb, and the curve shows the steep jump: an indicator must change inside it, so methyl orange, changing in the buffer region, gives a titre far too small. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Here's twenty five point zero zero millilitres of zero point one zero zero moles per litre ethanoic acid, titrated with sodium hydroxide of the same concentration. The moles say it needs twenty five millilitres. With phenolphthalein, that's what you get: the flask turns pink within a drop of twenty five. But run it with methyl orange, and the colour drifts from red, through orange, to yellow over the first eight millilitres. Same acid, same base. So why does one indicator get it right, and the other mislead you?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Bromothymol blue is a weak acid, HIn. HIn is yellow and In⁻ is blue. Its transition range is pH 6.0 to 7.6. A few drops of bromothymol blue are added to a solution at pH 4. Sodium hydroxide solution is added until the pH reaches 10, then hydrochloric acid is added until the pH returns to 4. Describe the colours observed, and explain them using Le Chatelier's principle." New indicator (its flask set is shown nowhere before the attempt; scene 4's ruler shows only its range band, coloured; A1 states both colours and the range, Revision 2, so "pH 4 is below the range" is decidable from the card), tests the reversible equilibrium of `C6-IQ1-02`. Crossed mistake: "the indicator is used up, so it stays blue". (A2) "A solution of 0.100 mol/L hydrochloric acid is added from a burette to 25.00 mL of 0.100 mol/L ammonia solution. Near the equivalence point, the pH falls sharply from about 6.6 to about 4.0. (a) Explain why the solution at the equivalence point is acidic. Include an equation. (b) Select the most suitable indicator from the table, and justify your choice." Table on the card: "methyl orange 3.1–4.4 (red to yellow) | methyl red 4.4–6.2 (red to yellow) | bromothymol blue 6.0–7.6 (yellow to blue) | phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0 (colourless to pink)". New titration type (strong acid with weak base, acid added to base; the worked example was weak acid with strong base). Crossed mistake: "phenolphthalein, the usual titration indicator" (site L17 error 5).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct an investigation to demonstrate the preparation and use of indicators as illustrators of the characteristics and properties of acids and bases and their reversible reactions (ACSCH101)" "investigate titration curves and conductivity graphs to analyse data to indicate characteristic reaction profiles, for example:; strong acid/strong base; strong acid/weak base; weak acid/strong base (ACSCH080, ACSCH102)" this video starts from the route's reversible indicator colour change and stops at separating the endpoint from the equivalence point and matching an indicator's transition range to the pH jump. It teaches: an indicator as a weak acid, HIn, whose two forms have different colours (C06 conjugate pair callback); the colour change as a reversible equilibrium shifted by added acid and base (Module 5 Le Chatelier callback, one clause), the "reversible reactions" demand of `C6-IQ1-02`; why the change spreads over roughly two pH units around the indicator's pKa (the C11 ratio idea, said in words, no new equation); four common transition ranges; endpoint against equivalence point (C12 callback, one line); salt hydrolysis: why the solution at equivalence is basic for a weak acid with a strong base, neutral for strong with strong and acidic for a strong acid with a weak base, and the memory aid "the salt takes after its stronger parent"; one worked equivalence pH (sodium ethanoate, through Kb = Kw ÷ Ka and the C08 weak-base method); the steep jump near equivalence and the selection rule (the colour change must fall inside the jump; the range need not contain the exact equivalence pH); why a wrong indicator gives a titre that is too small; the strong/strong case where all three common indicators work at 0.1 mol/L. Not here: preparing an indicator from red cabbage and calibrating it (chem-m6-p01, the next video, which owns the practical preparation and the investigation; this video shows use and reversibility only); reading whole titration curves (starting pH, buffer region, half-equivalence pKa, curve identification) and conductivity graphs (chem-m6-c14); weak acid with weak base titrations (site Extension; one author note); the direction of an amphiprotic ion from Ka against Kb (route Additions: chem-m6-g02); polyprotic curves and tartaric acid (site worksheet corrections); error-direction tables beyond "titre too small" (chem-m6-g04); back and conductometric titrations (chem-m6-c15).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout: H₃O⁺ teal token on pale blue water (C01); OH⁻ violet; indicator tokens: HIn white-outlined, In⁻ in the indicator's base colour (phenolphthalein magenta); the burette's titrant navy (C12); the ethanoic acid curve teal, the hydrochloric acid curve pale blue; each indicator's range band in its own two colours. Board layout (constant, C03, C07, C08 and C12): top-left the short task line; the left column holds the givens card during the worked example (grouped, units attached); the centre holds the lens, the ruler, the curve or the working, one stage per line, earlier lines dimming; a plate sits small at the right only when it carries the explanation. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends.
